The general rule requires every pair of consecutive alphabetic characters to alternate case, so the two uppercase alphabetic characters in required input 'N/A' fail; the canonical test simultaneously requires that line to be output.
Alternation is explicitly restricted to alphabetic characters per str.isalpha, making the check objectively defined for a given Python runtime.
Lines with fewer than two alphabetic characters are explicitly accepted, and original formatting is preserved; CLI and error semantics are consistent.
The predicate explicitly distinguishes only the code points '0' and 'O'; visually similar Unicode characters are unambiguously other characters and therefore satisfy the output condition.

The core rule is purely syntactic: treat only ASCII '0' and 'O' specially and accept any other non-whitespace character; visually similar Unicode characters are outside the exclusion set and thus unambiguous.
All required behaviors (filter condition, Unicode I/O, CLI, file-not-found handling) are precisely and consistently defined, so the contract is objectively certifiable.
Words and vowels are explicitly defined as non-whitespace runs and membership in a fixed Latin-character set, including for non-Latin text.
Vowels are explicitly fixed to the 10 Latin characters listed; for any word, checking membership in this set is deterministic regardless of script.
The requirement does not depend on a linguistic notion of vowels beyond this set, so the line filter, CLI, and error behaviors are all objectively defined and implementable.
The contract expressly delegates alphabetic classification to Python str.isalpha, making the unique-character count and Fibonacci predicate executable in the target runtime.
Alphabetic status is defined via Python's str.isalpha, which is a deterministic predicate in the target environment; Fibonacci membership of the resulting count is objectively checkable.
All other behaviors (line preservation, empty-line handling, CLI, file-not-found) are precise and feasible.
Although no line can satisfy the conjunction, always emitting the valid empty result satisfies the complete filtering contract.
The filter condition is logically unsatisfiable for any line, but the resulting behavior—always producing empty output for any input—is well-defined and implementable.
Impossibility of any line passing the predicate does not prevent implementation of the specified CLI contract with universally empty output.
No word count is both odd and even, but this merely makes the specified filter select no lines; empty output is a valid executable result.
No line can have a word count that is both odd and even, but a program can still implement the specified rule by never outputting any line.
The CLI, argument validation, and error-handling behaviors are precise and compatible with this always-empty-output semantics.
No uppercase-character count is both prime and a perfect square, but universally empty output remains a valid implementation of the filter.
